result.question: Research the validated psychology instruments and empirical findings needed to build a marriage/relationship compatibility assessment for an Indian audience. I need a rigorous, citable foundation document covering: (1) The Big Five / OCEAN personality model and the public-domain IPIP item pool — how facets are measured, sample items, and which traits and trait-combinations empirically predict relationship satisfaction and stability. (2) Adult attachment theory — secure/anxious/avoidant (and the ECR / ECR-R measures), and how attachment (dis)similarity predicts relationship outcomes. (3) John Gottman's research — the "Four Horsemen," conflict/communication patterns, bids, and what empirically predicts divorce vs stability. (4) Thomas-Kilmann conflict modes. (5) Schwartz Theory of Basic Human Values (the 10 values) and how value congruence predicts relationship satisfaction. (6) The Five Love Languages and what evidence does/doesn't support them. (7) Financial-values / "money scripts" research and financial (dis)agreement as a divorce predictor. (8) Empirical predictors of marital satisfaction and divorce specifically relevant to arranged/semi-arranged marriages and Indian/South-Asian cultural contexts (joint family, parental involvement, gender-role expectations, religion/caste). For each instrument, I need: what it measures, the sub-dimensions, how items are scored, example items, and the key empirical findings on how similarity/complementarity/difference on that dimension relates to relationship outcomes. The end goal is to design ~250 questions across 12 dimensions (Big Five personality, attachment style, conflict style, love languages, core values, financial mindset, family expectations, children/parenting, lifestyle, career ambitions, communication, religious/cultural) with defensible scoring.
result.summary: This foundation document assembles validated, citable psychology instruments and empirical findings for a 12-dimension marriage/relationship compatibility assessment. The strongest, most defensible measurement backbone is: the public-domain IPIP-NEO-120 for Big Five personality (5 domains, 30 facets, 4 items/facet), the ECR-R for adult attachment (36 items, two subscales — Anxiety and Avoidance — with documented reverse-keying and scoring), the Thomas-Kilmann model for conflict style (two dimensions, five modes), the Schwartz Theory of Basic Human Values (10 values in a circumplex, measured via the PVQ/SVS) for core values, and Gottman's Oral History Interview / Four Horsemen framework for divorce prediction. The single most important design lesson across dimensions is that for PERSONALITY, raw partner similarity does NOT reliably predict relationship satisfaction once each partner's own trait levels (actor/partner effects) are controlled — so scoring should weight desirable individual traits (low neuroticism, high agreeableness/conscientiousness/extraversion) and PERCEIVED/profile congruence rather than mechanical item-by-item similarity matching. Similarity's predictive value is real but conditional (it is moderated by attachment style, and matters more for values/attitudes than for Big Five traits), which the scoring model must reflect. Note: the verified claim pool covers personality, attachment, Gottman, TKI, Schwartz values, and love-language typology validation robustly, but returned NO verified claims on money scripts/financial disagreement, the Five Love Languages' predictive/efficacy evidence, or Indian/arranged-marriage-specific predictors — those dimensions remain evidence-gaps to fill before finalizing.

findings.claim: Big Five personality is best operationalized with the public-domain IPIP-NEO-120: 5 broad domains (Neuroticism, Extraversion, Conscientiousness, Agreeableness, Openness) and all 30 FFM facets, 4 items per facet, drawn from the free IPIP item pool (ipip.ori.org) with no copyright constraints.
findings.evidence: Johnson (2014, J. Research in Personality 51:78-89) developed a 120-item IPIP-NEO representing both 5 domains and 30 facets (4 items/facet = 120). Items are freely accessible/public-domain from ipip.ori.org. The 30 four-item facet scales showed acceptable reliability across two large Internet samples (Ns 307,313 and 619,150), facet alphas .63-.88 (all but 3 facets >= .69) — sufficient for research but not for high-stakes individual decisions. The original 300-item IPIP-NEO scales had mean alpha .80 (vs NEO PI-R .75) and correlated r=.73 (r=.94 disattenuated) with the NEO PI-R scales they proxy.

findings.claim: For personality scoring, weight desirable individual traits over partner-similarity: an individual's low neuroticism, high agreeableness, high conscientiousness, and high extraversion predict their PARTNER's relationship satisfaction (openness not significant).
findings.evidence: Malouff et al. (2010) meta-analysis of 19 samples (N=3,848 heterosexual partners) found four of five FFM traits in an individual significantly predict the partner's relationship satisfaction: low neuroticism, high agreeableness, high conscientiousness, high extraversion; openness was not significant. An earlier Heller, Watson & Iles (2004) meta-analysis of SELF-rated marital satisfaction found all five traits significant, neuroticism strongest (r=-.26), then agreeableness .24, conscientiousness .22, extraversion .14, openness .08 (self-report correlations may be inflated by common-method bias). Partner-effect coefficients in Malouff are modest (~.03-.22).

findings.claim: Raw personality similarity between partners is weak and does NOT by itself predict happier relationships once each partner's own trait levels are controlled — so avoid mechanical item-by-item personality similarity scoring.
findings.evidence: Assortative-mating between partners on Big Five traits is weak: between-partner correlations all below .25 and often non-significant (Collabra 2024), consistent with the Horwitz et al. (2023) ~23,000-couple meta-analysis (Extraversion .08, Neuroticism .10-.11, Agreeableness .11, Conscientiousness .16, Openness .21). There was 'little evidence to support the benefits of between-partner similarity for relationship quality after controlling for actor and partner effects.' Hudson & Fraley (2014) found no linear OR quadratic association between overall trait-similarity and satisfaction. Malouff/Shiota & Levenson (2007) confirm individual-trait congruence predicts satisfaction poorly.

findings.claim: Similarity is not worthless — but its value is conditional: overall FFM PROFILE congruence and self-vs-perceived-partner congruence DO correlate with satisfaction, and attachment style MODERATES the similarity-satisfaction link.
findings.evidence: Congruence between overall FFM profiles correlates with satisfaction (Gonzaga et al. 2007, emotion-mediated), and congruence between self-ratings and one's perception of the partner predicts satisfaction (Zentner 2005). Hudson & Fraley (2014): dismissing individuals (high avoidance/low anxiety) are most satisfied at MODERATE similarity; preoccupied individuals (high anxiety/low avoidance) most satisfied when partner is highly similar OR highly dissimilar. CAVEAT: the moderation was an exploratory, single-study, unreplicated finding on young DATING couples, and applied to PERCEIVED rather than actual similarity — cite as suggestive, not established.

findings.claim: Adult attachment is best measured with the ECR-R: 36 self-report items on two subscales — attachment-related Anxiety (fear of rejection/abandonment) and Avoidance (discomfort with intimacy, seeks independence).
findings.evidence: The ECR-R (Fraley, Waller & Brennan 2000) has 36 items scored 1 (Strongly Disagree) to 7 (Strongly Agree). Items 1-18 = anxiety scale, items 19-36 = avoidance scale; each subscale score is the average of its items. Reverse-key BEFORE averaging: anxiety items 9 and 11; avoidance items 20, 22, 26, 27, 28, 29, 30, 31, 33, 34, 35, 36. Validated by Sibley, Fischer & Liu (2005). IMPLEMENTATION NOTE: item numbers assume this fixed order; under randomized administration keying must track item content.

findings.claim: Insecure attachment is a measurable driver of destructive conflict behavior, linking the attachment and conflict-style dimensions.
findings.evidence: Fowler & Dillow (2011, N=170) found attachment orientations (anxiety, avoidance) predicted an average of 22% of the variance in the four horsemen behaviors (criticism, defensiveness, contempt, stonewalling) beyond relational satisfaction. IMPORTANT FRAMING CAVEATS: this was a cross-sectional self-report study — it shows regression PREDICTION, not a causal 'antecedent'; and it measured self-reported four-horsemen BEHAVIORS, not divorce/dissolution. A separate related claim that attachment anxiety is a STRONGER predictor than avoidance was REFUTED (0-3) and should not be relied on for dimension weighting.

findings.claim: Gottman's Oral History Interview / Four Horsemen framework is the empirically strongest divorce-vs-stability predictor and defines codeable conflict-perception dimensions.
findings.evidence: Carrère, Buehlman, Gottman et al. (2000, N=95 newlyweds): discriminant analysis of the Oral History Interview (coded in year 1) predicted married-vs-divorced status with 87.4% accuracy at Time 2 and 81% at Time 3. The OHI coding system taps eight subscales: 3 positive (Fondness/Affection, We-ness, Expansiveness), 2 negative (Negativity, Disappointment/Disillusionment), 3 conflict-handling (Chaos, Volatility, Glorifying the Struggle); coders score 6-9 items per subscale on a 5-point Likert scale. CAVEAT: sample was self-selected non-distressed with an 18% divorce rate; accuracy lower than Gottman's 1992 94% study.

findings.claim: Conflict style is best framed with the Thomas-Kilmann model: two independent dimensions (assertiveness, cooperativeness) yielding five modes — competing, collaborating, compromising, avoiding, accommodating.
findings.evidence: The TKI maps conflict-handling on assertiveness (satisfying one's own concerns) x cooperativeness (satisfying others' concerns), producing five modes. The official instrument uses 30 forced-choice item pairs; each mode is scored by counting selections (raw 0-12, five modes sum to 30), converted to percentiles partitioned into high (top 25%), medium (middle 50%), low (bottom 25%). Structure confirmed by co-creator Kilmann's site and the official publisher (Myers-Briggs Company). NOTE: the exact TKI items are copyrighted/licensed — the two-dimension/five-mode STRUCTURE is free to adapt, but do not copy proprietary items.

findings.claim: Core values should use the Schwartz Theory of Basic Human Values: 10 motivationally distinct values in a circumplex organized by two bipolar higher-order dimensions.
findings.evidence: Schwartz's theory identifies 10 values recognized across virtually all cultures (67+ nations): self-direction, stimulation, hedonism, achievement, power, security, conformity, tradition, benevolence, universalism. They form a circular structure on two bipolar dimensions — openness-to-change vs conservation (self-direction/stimulation vs security/conformity/tradition), and self-enhancement vs self-transcendence (power/achievement vs universalism/benevolence). Adjacent values are motivationally compatible; opposing values conflict; closer = more similar motivations. A refined 19-value extension (Schwartz 2012) exists but the 10-value model is the standard.

findings.claim: Values are measured with two validated instruments — the Schwartz Value Survey (SVS) and the Portrait Values Questionnaire (PVQ) — with the PVQ preferred for an assessment (less social-desirability bias, cognitively simpler).
findings.evidence: SVS: respondents rate 56-57 value items 'as a guiding principle in MY life' on a 9-point scale from -1 (opposed to my values) to 7 (of supreme importance). PVQ (Schwartz et al. 2001): 40 short verbal portraits (or 21 in the short version, used in the European Social Survey), gender-matched, rated 'How much like you is this person?' on a 6-point Likert scale (1=not like me at all to 6=very much like me). Each value's score = average of its marker items. The PVQ is less subject to social-desirability bias (measures values indirectly) and is more concrete/context-bound/cognitively simpler than the SVS — better suited to a broad-audience compatibility test. Value congruence can be adapted to a couple-level measure (Danioni et al. 2023).

findings.claim: The Five Love Languages typology has empirical support for its five categories as a descriptive taxonomy (with a possible sixth), but the verified evidence does NOT establish that matching love languages improves relationships.
findings.evidence: An inductive qualitative study (324 college participants, 648 open-ended responses; Communication Reports 2022) found empirical support for all five original categories (words of affirmation, quality time, gifts, acts of service, physical touch), plus an emergent sixth ('check-ins'). Words of affirmation was most frequent (45.7%); gifts and physical touch least (16.4% each — these exact percentages are from paywalled full text and could not be independently reconfirmed). CRITICAL SCOPE LIMIT: this validates the CATEGORIES only. The separate, disputed efficacy claim — that partner love-language MATCHING improves relationships (challenged by Impett et al. 2024) — was NOT verified here. Treat love languages as a descriptive/communication dimension, not as a validated matching-based predictor.
findings.vote: claim [23] (3-0); efficacy claim not in verified pool

result.caveats: EVIDENCE GAPS (dimensions requested but with NO verified claims in this pool): (1) Financial-values / 'money scripts' research and financial disagreement as a divorce predictor — a core requested dimension with zero verified support here; must be sourced separately (e.g., Klontz money-scripts inventory; Dew, Britt & Huston on financial disagreement predicting divorce). (2) Indian / arranged / semi-arranged marriage and South-Asian cultural predictors (joint family, parental involvement, gender-role expectations, religion/caste) — NO verified claims returned; this is the highest-priority gap and the most culturally load-bearing part of the brief. (3) The Five Love Languages EFFICACY/matching evidence (does matching help?) was not verified — only category validity was. SOURCE-QUALITY / TIME notes: most findings rest on peer-reviewed primary sources and are foundational/stable (personality, attachment, Schwartz, TKI, Gottman are decades-established and not time-sensitive). Weaker spots: claim [4] (Heller 2004 correlations) was a 2-1 split and self-report correlations may be inflated by common-method bias; claim [8] (attachment->four-horsemen) was 2-1 and is cross-sectional/correlational, NOT causal and NOT about divorce; claim [15] (attachment moderates similarity) was 2-1, exploratory, single-study, unreplicated, on young dating couples; the love-language percentages [23] come from paywalled text and could not be independently reconfirmed. REFUTED (do not use): the claim that attachment anxiety is a STRONGER predictor of destructive conflict than avoidance failed verification 0-3 — do not weight the anxiety dimension as dominant on that basis. SCORING DESIGN IMPLICATION: for the Big Five personality dimension, weight desirable individual trait levels and profile/perceived congruence rather than mechanical item-by-item similarity; similarity-based scoring is more defensible for VALUES and attitudes than for personality traits. LICENSING: IPIP items and the Schwartz/ECR-R scoring are freely usable/public-domain or academically documented, but the exact TKI items are proprietary/licensed — adapt the two-dimension/five-mode structure, do not reproduce TKI items; Chapman's Five Love Languages branding is likewise commercially owned.
openQuestions: What validated financial-values / money-scripts instrument and what empirical effect size links financial disagreement to divorce, and can it be adapted for an Indian income/joint-finance context? (No verified evidence returned — must be researched before building the financial-mindset dimension.)

What are the empirically supported predictors of marital satisfaction and stability specific to Indian/South-Asian arranged and semi-arranged marriages (joint family living, parental involvement, gender-role congruence, religion/caste endogamy)? This entire culturally-central dimension has no verified backing in the current pool.

Does actually MATCHING partners on love languages improve outcomes, or only category validity hold? The efficacy evidence (and the Impett et al. 2024 critique) needs verification before love-language matching is used in scoring.

For value/attitude congruence (where similarity DOES appear to matter more than for personality), what is the defensible quantitative rule — difference thresholds, profile correlation, or higher-order-dimension distance — to convert Schwartz PVQ scores into a couple compatibility score?

refuted.claim: Attachment anxiety is a stronger predictor of destructive conflict behaviors than attachment avoidance, meaning an assessment weighting the anxiety dimension should expect the largest effect on criticism/defensiveness/contempt/stonewalling outcomes.
